paras: The reported lynching of James Atkinson was a rumor, carried by several newspapers in July 1881, that a man held in the jail at Gayoso, Pemiscot County, Missouri, on a charge of murdering his wife and infant child had been taken out at night and lynched. Later reports contradicted it: in late July and again in late August Atkinson was described as alive in the Gayoso jail, with his trial set for September.

According to the Gayoso Democrat, as reprinted in the Chicago Tribune, Atkinson's marriage to a daughter of the Batsell family was unhappy, and his wife had left him in April, taking their infant son. After she went back to his house with the baby on a Sunday early in July, both were found dead in the Mississippi River, the woman with marks of violence on her body. Neighbors pointed to a woman's shoe tracks leading to the river, a barefoot track returning and the wife's shoes hidden in the house, and the New Madrid Record reported that Atkinson had small feet and could wear her shoes.

Atkinson fled, and the county judges offered a $600 reward for his capture. Men from Cottonwood Point captured him on the river on July 10 and delivered him to the sheriff of Pemiscot County at Gayoso. His parents, Appleton Atkinson and his wife, and two younger brothers were arrested as accessories, and his father was committed to jail without bail.

On July 18 a dispatch from New Madrid stated that "it is reported" Atkinson had been taken from the Gayoso jail "last night and lynched." It gave no details of who took him, how many there were, or how he was killed. Versions of the item placed the event on the night of July 17 or on Monday night, July 18.

On July 23 the Osceola Times of Arkansas reported that Atkinson "is now in jail at Gayoso," without mention of a lynching. A correspondent writing from Tiptonville, Tennessee, on August 22 said the excitement over the case had abated and that Atkinson and his father were both in jail at Gayoso, to be tried there in the second week of September. No report of the trial's result was found in the coverage.

The arrest first reached the press through a St. Louis wire of July 15, printed in Illinois, Tennessee, West Virginia and other papers under headlines such as "A Heartless Deed" and "Wife Murderer Arrested." The New Madrid lynching report ran in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier under "Lynch Law for a Murderer" and in the Dallas Daily Herald, both calling Atkinson "the murderer" while hedging the lynching as a report. The Lexington Intelligencer in Missouri carried it as a one-sentence brief, and the Hickman Courier reprinted it from the St. Louis Chronicle on July 29 under "Lynched."

The Hickman Courier, across the river in Kentucky, followed the case most closely, since the dead woman's family had once lived in Hickman. A week before reprinting the lynching rumor it printed the Atkinson family's version, in which the wife poisoned herself and her child, and his claim that he fled because people "would mob him before the real facts could be brought out." No paper in the coverage retracted the lynching report, and none gave Atkinson's race.

The lynching rests on a single hedged New Madrid dispatch, while the Osceola Times and the Tiptonville letter, the later and nearer sources, placed Atkinson alive in jail. The cause of the deaths was also disputed: the Batsell side and the Gayoso Democrat described a killing, while Atkinson's family said the wife had poisoned herself and her child.

bases: The only collective violence in the coverage is a reported jail lynching of a prisoner charged with murder (A7, A8, A10, A12), which later reports contradict (A11, A15).

The lynching appears only as a hedged rumor ('it is reported') in a New Madrid dispatch (A7, A8, A10, A12); a later letter from Tiptonville, twenty miles away, reported Atkinson and his father alive in jail at Gayoso awaiting a September trial (A15), as did the Osceola Times (A11), so the papers do not support that he was killed.
The New Madrid lynching report ran in several papers (A7, A8, A10, A12), but the Osceola Times (A11) and a Tiptonville letter of Aug. 22 (A15) place Atkinson alive in the Gayoso jail.

framing.detail: The New Madrid special ran under 'Lynch Law for a Murderer' and as a St. Louis item, calling Atkinson 'the murderer' and hedging the lynching as 'reported'.
The Lexington Intelligencer ran the report as a one-sentence news brief among unrelated items.
The Hickman Courier, near the scene, first told the case against the husband, then printed his family's defense, then reprinted the lynching report under 'Lynched'.
